thread.title: Even ‘Canary in the Coal Mine’ Indicators Say This Bull Market Is Mostly Healthy

author: Reshma Kapadia
title: Even ‘Canary in the Coal Mine’ Indicators Say This Bull Market Is Mostly Healthy
text:
Illustration: David Cairns/Daily Express/Getty Images By Reshma Kapadia Sept. 12, 2018 10:48 a.m. ET Ten years after the start of a global financial crisis , some strategists are checking in with their go-to “canaries in the coal mine” to get a gut-check as U.S. stocks push higher and confidence in the economy grows.
The result is a mixed bag, with two of three strategists still in the bull camp and another seeing reasons for worry. Here’s a round up:
Ed Yardeni of Yardeni Research writes in a note that he is troubled by the “proliferating emerging-markets crisis,” which is weighing on one of his favorite global economic indicators: The CRB raw industrial spot price index . Though the index is down 8% from its high this year in June, other indicators like his boom-bust barometer, remains near record highs. Plus, consumers are still upbeat and earnings remain “fundamentally” bullish. His takeaway: The global economy may be hampered by the turmoil in emerging markets, but the U.S. labor market is booming.
Yardeni’s “most reliable coal-mine canary” for recessions and bear markets – the ratio of the S&P 500 Financials stock price index to the S&P 500 – delivers a similar message. The ratio is up 1% so far this year, suggesting the emerging-markets crisis isn’t yet a problem for the U.S. financial system.
DataTrek Research co-founder Nicholas Colas also gives bulls some comfort after checking in with his five indicators.
• The dollar has rallied 8% from the middle of April through the middle of August, hitting a one-year high, but has since lost steam. Colas writes that there are still plenty of people bullish on the dollar, but its recent loss of momentum is good for U.S. stocks. Though that should help emerging markets, that’s not the case as they continue to grapple with other issues, such as trade. (Another one of those, “It’s not our problem but yours.”)
• The calm in the U.S. long-term treasury bond market doesn’t scream crisis. “Even as the short end of the Treasury yield curve continues to post fresh post-Financial Crisis highs for yields, the long end just shrugs,” Colas writes. “Long-term Treasuries remain the unsung heroes of the current bull market in U.S. equities, so it is important the current low-volatility regime remains in place.”
• Italian sovereign debt is a good marker for Eurozone risk, with Colas describing Italian bonds as the weakest link in the Eurozone chain and most vulnerable if the euro eventually fails.
“While the spreads over German paper are still wide for Italian sovereign debt, they are at least heading in the right direction of late,” Colas writes. “Two-year yields have been cut in half since late August, and 10-year yields are down by 50 basis points.” He adds that the moves were a reassuring sign considering Italy is about to release its closely watched 2019 budget.
• TED Spreads at 25 basis points is good news. As the Federal Reserve raises rates, investors have been worried it will spark a flood of dollars coming back home from abroad. A measure of the effect of these flows on global dollar availability is to look at three-month London Interbank Offered Rate (Libor) rates compared with three-month Treasuries, Colas writes. Today’s 25 basis-points spread is much narrower than the 64 basis points it hit in April and close to where it was in December before the troubles in emerging markets.
• U.S. corporate-bond spreads are an indicator of investors’ appetite for risk in credit markets. If investors start demanding larger spreads for corporate credit because of cyclical or secular issues, equity markets should be concerned. But so far, Colas sees no signs of trouble, with investment-grade bond spreads over Treasuries hovering near the average at the beginning of the year while high-yield spreads are below 2018 highs and where they started at the beginning of the year.
Bank of America Merrill Lynch global strategist Michael Hartnett isn’t as sanguine and sees several trouble spots.
• In his note this week, Hartnett says the investment-grade BBB bonds – his canaries – have lost 3.2% annually, the worst showing since 1998. Flows also suggest credit markets cracking, with investment-grade bonds seeing their biggest outflows since December 2016.
• Looking at the FAANG and BAT stocks – or Facebook (FB), Apple (AAPL), Amazon.com (AMZN), Netflix (NFLX), and Alphabet (GOOGL), and their Chinese counterparts, Baidu (BIDU), Alibaba Group Holding (BABA) and Tencent Holdings (0700.Hong Kong) –Hartnett notes that half are in bear-market territory, down 20%. “True global contagion in 2018 ends with investors selling what they own and love,” he writes. That may be coming soon, with Hartnett noting that tech inflows appear to be turning and may have peaked.
• In emerging markets, 809 of 1150 stocks are in bear-market territory, down 20% from highs. But he sees more pain ahead since investors have not yet thrown in the towel. Less than 20% of the flows into emerging-market debt and equity has been redeemed so far, he says.
It may be wise to stay attuned going forward, and making sure these market canaries are still singing.
